report.source_text: We performed a total colonoscopy and detected a small protruding lesion in the transverse colon (Figure 3). The tumour was very small, with a diameter of only about 12 mm, and contained a depressed component, leading to a diagnosis of macroscopic type with 0-Is+IIc according to the Paris classification [8]. Furthermore, the severely thickened stalk and irregular pits visible in a magnified image of the depressed area combined to suggest direct invasion of the deep submucosa (Figure 3C) [9].

report.source_text: A diagnostic endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) was performed and the specimen removed was serially dissected into three sections and examined. The tumour was composed of poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma and signet-ring cell carcinoma (Figure 4). It primarily consisted of solidly proliferated cells, but exhibited some indistinct gland formation. The tumour had a preserved intramucosal component but infiltrated deeply into the submucosal layer, with severe lymphatic and venous invasion detected the submucosal layer. The vertical and horizontal cut ends of the resected tumour were both positive for cancer cells (Figure 4).

report.source_text: IHC studies showed strong expression of MUC5AC, and weak expression of MUC2 and CDX2; indicating the tumour having a mixed gastric and intestinal character, with the gastric phenotype being predominant. Patients with advanced colorectal cancer with gastric phenotypes have been reported to frequently exhibit lymphatic permeation and lymph node metastasis [10]. Additionally, the tumour was positive for CK20 and slightly positive for CK7. There was no evidence of differentiation to endocrine tumour or hepatoid adenocarcinoma (Figure 5).

report.source_text: We reevaluated the lymph node biopsy specimen obtained by the referring hospital. The tumour cells with oval to round nuclei with prominent nucleoli were found to be showing partial ductal structures, leading us to suspect poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Additionally, immunohistochemistry (IHC) studies showed the biopsy specimen to be negative for cytokeratin 7 (CK7), and positive for CDX2, an intestine-specific homeobox transcription factor, and cytokeratin 20 (CK20), a cytoskeletal protein usually found in the colonic epithelium. These IHC results strongly suggested the metastasis from a primary colorectal cancer (Figure 2).

report.source_text: The patient was referred to the Gastrointestinal Oncology Division, where she underwent combination chemotherapy using capecitabine (Xeloda® ) plus oxaliplatin (Elplat® ) and bevacizumab (Avastin® ), which is one of the standard therapy of metastatic colon cancer. After 4 courses, CT scan showed a significant reduction of tumour volume, but after 10 courses, the tumour marker rapidly increased and peritoneal metastasis progressed.

clinician.final_diagnosis: small primary colon cancer with systemic metastasis
clinician.trajectory_summary: 35-year-old woman presented with left cervical lymphadenopathy initially suspected to be malignant lymphoma. Aspiration cytology revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma, prompting evaluation for primary breast cancer (negative mammography/ultrasonography) and upper GI malignancy (negative endoscopy). CT demonstrated systemic lymphadenopathy (left supraclavicular and para-aortic) without identifiable primary. Colonoscopy identified a 12mm protruding lesion with depressed component (0-Is+IIc) in the transverse colon. Endoscopic mucosal resection revealed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with signet-ring cell features, deep submucosal invasion, lymphovascular invasion, and positive margins. Immunohistochemistry of the colon primary showed strong MUC5AC, weak MUC2/CDX2, CK20 positivity, and slight CK7 positivity (mixed gastric/intestinal phenotype). Reevaluation of the cervical lymph node biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with IHC profile (CK7 negative, CDX2 positive, CK20 positive) confirming colorectal origin. The patient received first-line chemotherapy for metastatic colon cancer (capecitabine, oxaliplatin, bevacizumab) with initial tumor reduction after 4 courses, followed by progression with peritoneal metastasis after 10 courses. KRAS testing revealed wild-type status, and second-line therapy with cetuximab plus irinotecan resulted in significant tumor marker decrease after 4 administrations.
